claims.evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis in epigenetic mutants.

claims.claim: Many genes encoding components of the DNA methylation and demethylation pathways were sensitive to hyperosmotic salt treatment.
claims.source: We then assessed the transcriptional response of genes encoding components of the DNA methylation and demethylation pathways and found that many of them were sensitive to hyperosmotic salt treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis of epigenetic pathway genes.

claims.claim: Methylation at regions corresponding to HS-DMRs was severely affected in met1 and rdd mutants.
claims.source: Moreover, analysis of epigenomic data for RdDM and demethylation mutants (Stroud et al., 2013) revealed that methylation at regions corresponding to HS-DMRs from our data set was severely affected in met1 and rdd mutants (Fischer's Exact test p=0,005) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of published epigenomic data for mutants.

claims.claim: CNI1 sense transcription in both T-DNA insertion alleles was misregulated in response to stress.
claims.source: We therefore analysed the effects of two independent mutant alleles, in which T-DNAs were inserted between the CNI1 transcription unit and the downstream HS-DMR, possibly impeding communication between the HS-DMR and the CNI1 locus (Figure 6A). As expected, CNI1 sense transcription in both insertion alleles was misregulated in response to stress (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis in insertion mutants.

claims.claim: Deletion of the HS-DMR sequence reduced downregulation of sense CNI1 transcripts in response to hyperosmotic stress.
claims.source: To demonstrate the functional relevance of the sequence targeted epigenetically after hyperosmotic-stress, we generated a deletion line (Δcni1-DMR) using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing (Jinek et al., 2012) (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Deletion of the HS-DMR sequence reduced downregulation of sense CNI1 transcripts in response to hyperosmotic stress (Figure 6C), indicating that this HS-DMR acts as a distant regulatory element.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis in CRISPR deletion mutants.

claims.claim: The CNI1 HS-DMR acts as a distant regulatory element.
claims.source: Deletion of the HS-DMR sequence reduced downregulation of sense CNI1 transcripts in response to hyperosmotic stress (Figure 6C), indicating that this HS-DMR acts as a distant regulatory element.
claims.evidence: The manuscript infers from deletion mutant data the regulatory function of the HS-DMR.

claims.claim: Methylation in IR hairpin transgenic lines remained even under hyperosmotic stress.
claims.source: Finally, to demonstrate directly that the methylation status of this element determines its activity, we introduced an inverted repeat (IR) hairpin (Matzke et al., 2002) that directs DNA methylation to the CNI1 HS-DMR by RdDM (Figure 6A). McrBC assays and bisulfite sequencing confirmed that methylation in IR hairpin transgenic lines remained even under hyperosmotic stress (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents methylation analysis in transgenic lines.

claims.claim: Levels of CNI1 sense transcript in response to stress were no longer reduced in IR hairpin transgenic plants.
claims.source: Levels of CNI1 sense transcript in response to stress were no longer reduced in these plants (Figure 6D), thus strengthening the argument that the CNI1 HS-DMR acts as an epigenetically sensitive regulatory element.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis in transgenic lines.

claims.claim: The CNI1 HS-DMR acts as an epigenetically sensitive regulatory element.
claims.source: Levels of CNI1 sense transcript in response to stress were no longer reduced in these plants (Figure 6D), thus strengthening the argument that the CNI1 HS-DMR acts as an epigenetically sensitive regulatory element.
claims.evidence: The manuscript concludes from transgenic and mutant data the regulatory function of the HS-DMR.

claims.claim: Hyperosmotic stress increased expression of a lncRNA (CNI1-AS1) that is transcribed in the antisense direction and overlaps with CNI1 in control plants.
claims.source: We found that hyperosmotic stress increased expression of a lncRNA that is transcribed in the antisense direction and overlaps with CNI1, both in control plants (CNI1-AS1) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) and in the progeny of plants that had gone through our control non-salt conditions (p-value 0.004; Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents lncRNA expression analysis.

claims.claim: Hyperosmotic stress reduced expression of CNI1-AS1 lncRNA in progeny of plants exposed to hyperosmotic stress.
claims.source: By contrast, hyperosmotic stress reduced expression of this lncRNA in progeny of plants exposed to hyperosmotic stress (p-value 0.015; Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents lncRNA expression analysis showing priming effects.

claims.claim: The hyperosmotic responsiveness of CNI1-AS1 was impaired in progeny of rdd mutants.
claims.source: That this was linked to differential methylation was indicated by the hyperosmotic responsiveness of CNI1-AS1 being impaired in progeny of rdd mutants (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents lncRNA expression analysis in mutants.

claims.claim: In the two insertion alleles and in the deletion line, the stress-mediated transcriptional response of CNI1-AS1 was altered.
claims.source: In the two insertion alleles and in the deletion line, the stress-mediated transcriptional response was similarly altered (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents lncRNA expression analysis in mutants.

claims.claim: The HS-DMR downstream of CNI1 acts as an epigenetic sensor that controls CNI1 expression by modulating the expression of an antisense lncRNA.
claims.source: These data support a model in which the HS-DMR downstream of CNI1 acts as an epigenetic sensor that controls CNI1 expression by modulating the expression of an antisense lncRNA.
claims.evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic model based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: lncRNA expression was insensitive to hyperosmotic stress in IR hairpin lines.
claims.source: Our finding that lncRNA expression was insensitive to hyperosmotic stress in IR hairpin lines (Figure 6G) adds further weight to this model.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents lncRNA expression analysis in transgenic lines supporting the proposed model.

claims.claim: Only stress-responsive genes adjacent to HS-DMRs (not MA-DMRs) were enriched for hyperosmotic-responsive antisense lncRNAs.
claims.source: To investigate whether there might be a broader role for lncRNAs in mediating the effects of stress induced DMRs, we comparatively analysed all stress-responsive genes adjacent to HS-DMRs and to MA-DMRs. Only the first group was enriched for hyperosmotic-responsive antisense lncRNAs (Fisher's Exact test, p=0.008) (Supplementary file 6), indicating that HS-DMRs preferentially act as regulatory elements of stress-induced antisense lncRNAs.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents statistical analysis comparing HS-DMRs and MA-DMRs.

claims.claim: HS-DMRs preferentially act as regulatory elements of stress-induced antisense lncRNAs.
claims.source: Only the first group was enriched for hyperosmotic-responsive antisense lncRNAs (Fisher's Exact test, p=0.008) (Supplementary file 6), indicating that HS-DMRs preferentially act as regulatory elements of stress-induced antisense lncRNAs.
claims.evidence: The manuscript infers from enrichment analysis the regulatory role of HS-DMRs.

claims.claim: Intergenerational priming responses to hyperosmotic stress are triggered by recurrent exposure to stimuli, but this response is rapidly lost in the absence of stress.
claims.source: Our main conclusion is that intergenerational priming responses to hyperosmotic stress are triggered by recurrent exposure to stimuli, but that this response is rapidly lost in the absence of stress.
claims.evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: Hyperosmotic stress directs DNA methylation changes primarily to discrete genome regions that are rich in TE-related sequences.
claims.source: Bycontrast, using our highly controlled and replicated syste, and a strict method for detecting methylated regions, we found no clear evidence for such indiscriminate changes. Instead, we found that hyperosmotic stress directs DNA methylation changes primarily to discrete genome regions that are rich in TE-related sequences (Figures 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: The manuscript contrasts their findings with previous reports and summarizes their observations.

claims.claim: The dynamic DNA methylation changes are of functional consequence because the adaptive response is impaired in mutants defective in DNA methylation pathways.
claims.source: The dynamic DNA methylation changes are of functional consequence because the adaptive response is impaired in mutants defective in DNA methylation pathways (Figure 1), which are also known to regulate TE activity (Kim and Zilberman, 2014).
claims.evidence: The manuscript infers functional significance from mutant phenotype data.

claims.claim: A small fraction of acquired epigenetic changes is transmitted to the immediate offspring only after recurrent stress exposure, but in the absence of a renewed stimulus these are reset in subsequent generations.
claims.source: A small fraction of acquired epigenetic changes is transmitted to the immediate offspring only after recurrent stress exposure, but in the absence of a renewed stimulus these are reset in subsequent generations.
claims.evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about the transgenerational dynamics of epigenetic changes.

claims.claim: Epigenetic stress memory in annual plant species may be transient in nature.
claims.source: This implies that epigenetic stress memory in annual plant species may be transient in nature, however this response may differ in perennial plants that grow over longer periods of time before producing any offspring or in plants that reproduce asexually.
claims.evidence: The manuscript speculates about the broader implications of their findings.

claims.claim: Half of the newly acquired methylation changes identified in stressed plants overlapped with regions privileged for epimutation also found in near-isogenic greenhouse-grown populations.
claims.source: Half of the newly acquired methylation changes identified in our stressed plants overlapped with regions privileged for epimutation also found in near-isogenic greenhouse-grown populations (Figure 2) (Hagmann et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents comparative analysis with published MA line data.

claims.claim: Distinct regions of the plant epigenome are particularly labile, and such acquired epimutations could modulate the ability of plants to respond to stress.
claims.source: This finding confirms that distinct regions of the plant epigenome are particularly labile, and it suggests that such acquired epimutations could modulate the ability of plants to respond to stress.
claims.evidence: The manuscript interprets the overlap with MA-DMRs to support the concept of epigenetically labile regions.

claims.claim: Enhanced stress responses were only passed on after two consecutive generations of stress exposure, but not when plants were exposed to hyperosmotic stress for only one episode.
claims.source: Importantly, in our system, enhanced stress responses were only passed on after two consecutive generations of stress exposure, but not when plants were exposed to hyperosmotic stress for only one episode, which may be the reason why previous studies often failed to find clear evidence for inheritance of stress-induced epigenetic changes (Eichten and Springer, 2015; Secco et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The manuscript explains their findings in the context of previous studies.

claims.claim: Repeated stress exposure being required for induction of transiently heritable stress resistance may reside in the importance of poised epigenetic states for environmental priming.
claims.source: One explanation for repeated stress exposure being required for induction of transiently heritable stress resistance may reside in the importance of poised epigenetic states for environmental priming (Jaskiewicz et al., 2011; Sani et al., 2013), which in turn may facilitate the establishment of new epigenetic marks at discrete genomic regions that are sensitive to stress.
claims.evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic explanation based on published concepts.

claims.claim: There is substantial overlap (>30%) between HS-DMRs established in recurrently stressed generations and dynamic chromatin occupancy directed by hyperosmosis.
claims.source: This view is supported by the substantial overlap (>30%) between HS-DMRs established in recurrently stressed generations (Figure 2) and dynamic chromatin occupancy directed by hyperosmosis (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents overlap analysis supporting their mechanistic explanation.

claims.claim: Recurrent exposure to hyperosmotic stress did not significantly increase the number of newly acquired epimutations.
claims.source: Intriguingly, recurrent exposure to hyperosmotic stress did not significantly increase the number of newly acquired epimutations, suggesting that the extent of epigenetic plasticity elicited by the environment is limited to a few key genomic regions that may be under purifying selection (Hollister and Gaut, 2009).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports observations about the number of epimutations across generations.

claims.claim: The extent of epigenetic plasticity elicited by the environment is limited to a few key genomic regions that may be under purifying selection.
claims.source: Intriguingly, recurrent exposure to hyperosmotic stress did not significantly increase the number of newly acquired epimutations, suggesting that the extent of epigenetic plasticity elicited by the environment is limited to a few key genomic regions that may be under purifying selection (Hollister and Gaut, 2009).
claims.evidence: The manuscript infers evolutionary implications from the observation about limited epigenetic plasticity.

claims.claim: Certain genomic regions are epigenetically targeted, depending on the type of stress because the DNA methylation changes induced by hyperosmotic stress did not overlap with methylation changes reported for other abiotic stresses.
claims.source: It is likely that certain genomic regions are epigenetically targeted, depending on the type of stress because the DNA methylation changes induced by hyperosmotic stress did not overlap with methylation changes reported for other abiotic stresses (Seymour et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The manuscript infers stress-specificity from lack of overlap with other stress studies.

claims.claim: Hyperosmotic priming responses were transmitted primarily through the maternal germline.
claims.source: Our analyses revealed that hyperosmotic priming responses were transmitted primarily through the maternal germline (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from reciprocal cross experiments.

claims.claim: Most of the stress-associated methylation changes in leaves were largely absent in mature male gametes.
claims.source: We attribute this difference to differences in the meiotic transmission of newly acquired DNA methylation marks. In support of this hypothesis, most of the stress-associated methylation changes in leaves were largely absent in mature male gametes (Figure 4), indicating that environmentally directed epigenetic marks are more efficiently reset in male rather than in female gametes.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents methylome data from male gametes supporting parent-of-origin effects.

claims.claim: Environmentally directed epigenetic marks are more efficiently reset in male rather than in female gametes.
claims.source: In support of this hypothesis, most of the stress-associated methylation changes in leaves were largely absent in mature male gametes (Figure 4), indicating that environmentally directed epigenetic marks are more efficiently reset in male rather than in female gametes.
claims.evidence: The manuscript infers differential resetting between male and female gametes from methylome data.

claims.claim: Male gametes undergo an active reprogramming of DNA methylation at transposon sequences by the DNA glycosylase DME.
claims.source: Indeed, not only do male gametes undergo an active reprogramming of DNA methylation at transposon sequences by the DNA glycosylase DME (Borges et al., 2012a; Ibarra et al., 2012), but also at stress-dependent DNA methylation sites (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites published literature and presents their own data about DME function.

claims.claim: The enhanced tolerance to hyperosmotic stress in progeny of stressed dme-6 plants implicates DNA demethylation both in the active reprogramming of TEs and in the resetting of environmentally-directed epigenetic changes in male gametes.
claims.source: Moreover, the enhanced tolerance to hyperosmotic stress in progeny of stressed dme-6 plants implicates DNA demethylation both in the active reprogramming of TEs and in the resetting of environmentally-directed epigenetic changes in male gametes.
claims.evidence: The manuscript infers dual roles of DME from mutant phenotype data.

claims.claim: Female gametes reside on the mother plant where they are eventually fertilised by sperm from pollen that may have travelled a great distance from its male progenitor to produce seed.
claims.source: One explanation is that female gametes reside on the mother plant where they are eventually fertilised by sperm from pollen that may have travelled a great distance from its male progenitor to produce seed.
claims.evidence: The manuscript draws on general biological knowledge about plant reproduction.

claims.claim: Given that seed dispersal usually occurs at a short distance from the mother, a solely maternal transmission of the newly acquired epigenetic marks would be an efficient way of retaining only the most relevant parental stress-associated adaptive responses in the progeny.
claims.source: Given that seed dispersal usually occurs at a short distance from the mother, a solely maternal transmission of the newly acquired epigenetic marks would be an efficient way of retaining only the most relevant parental stress-associated adaptive responses in the progeny.
claims.evidence: The manuscript proposes an evolutionary explanation for maternal transmission based on ecological reasoning.

claims.claim: Environmentally-induced priming responses involve DNA (de)methylation pathways that control the extent to which acquired epigenetic states are inherited and maintained in successive generations.
claims.source: Our study has revealed that environmentally-induced priming responses involve DNA (de)methylation pathways that control the extent to which acquired epigenetic states are inherited and maintained in successive generations (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about the role of DNA methylation pathways.

claims.claim: Stress can specifically alter methylation at the adjacent sequences of several key stress-response regulators.
claims.source: We now provide compelling evidence that stress can specifically alter methylation at the adjacent sequences of several key stress-response regulators (Figures 2, 5 and 6), a process that is mediated by the RdDM and DNA demethylation pathways (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about targeted methylation changes at regulatory genes.

claims.claim: Some TEs proximal to upstream regions and sensitive to methylation changes directed by hyperosmotic stress have regulatory roles.
claims.source: Targeted studies have revealed that some TEs proximal to upstream regions and sensitive to methylation changes directed by hyperosmotic stress have regulatory roles (Baek et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2015) and are associated with quantitative traits and adaptive behaviour (Baxter et al., 2012; Busoms et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites published literature about regulatory roles of TEs.

claims.claim: Both DNA methylation and demethylation activities are tightly regulated by the action of adjacent upstream TEs that act as an epigenetic sensors.
claims.source: Notably, both DNA methylation and demethylation activities are also tightly regulated by the action of adjacent upstream TEs that act as an epigenetic sensors (Lei et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites published literature about TE-mediated regulation of epigenetic pathways.

claims.claim: HS-DMRs are preferentially associated with the transcription of antisense lncRNAs.
claims.source: The epigenetic regulation of HS-DMRs is not always associated with upstream regulatory sequences and sense transcription; instead we found that they are preferentially associated with the transcription of antisense lncRNAs (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about the association between HS-DMRs and lncRNAs.

claims.claim: Antisense lncRNAs have been implicated in directing chromatin changes.
claims.source: Although the functions of these HS-DMR-associated non-coding transcripts are largely unknown, antisense lncRNAs have been implicated in directing chromatin changes (Ariel et al., 2014; Heo and Sung, 2011; Swiezewski et al., 2009), and thereby in influencing transcription, splicing and transcript stability (Bardou et al., 2014; Borsani et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites published literature about lncRNA functions.

claims.claim: Antisense lncRNAs were shown to be regulated by epigenetically labile control elements sensitive to stress.
claims.source: In this study,antisense lncRNAs were shown to be regulated by epigenetically labile control elements sensitive to stress (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The manuscript summarizes their findings about lncRNA regulation.

claims.claim: Methylation changes in HS-DMR genome regions could modulate transcription factor binding or chromatin regulatory loops.
claims.source: Methylation changes in these genome regions could modulate transcription factor binding (Zhong et al., 2013) or chromatin regulatory loops (Ariel et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The manuscript speculates about mechanisms based on published literature.

claims.claim: The adaptive value of epigenetic inheritance over multiple generations must depend on the cost of epigenetic resetting, as well as on the degree and predictability of environmental stress.
claims.source: The adaptive value of this inheritance over multiple generations must depend on the cost of epigenetic resetting, as well as on the degree and predictability of environmental stress (Herman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The manuscript discusses evolutionary considerations based on published theoretical work.

claims.claim: An adaptive bet-hedging strategy that is mediated by increased epigenetic variation could be advantageous in highly stochastic natural environments.
claims.source: Because conditions in many natural environments are highly stochastic, an adaptive bet-hedging strategy (Simons, 2011) that is mediated by increased epigenetic variation could be advantageous.
claims.evidence: The manuscript discusses evolutionary implications based on published theory.

claims.claim: Under controlled stress conditions, the contribution of adaptive epigenetic variation shows parental effects, which may be favoured over bet-hedging in relatively stable environments.
claims.source: Under our controlled stress conditions, the contribution of adaptive epigenetic variation shows parental effects (Figure 4), which may be favoured over bet-hedging in relatively stable environments (Kuijper and Johnstone, 2016).
claims.evidence: The manuscript discusses evolutionary implications of their findings based on published theory.

results.result: Repeated hyperosmotic stress over multiple generations (G2-G5) induces transient adaptive phenotypes in Arabidopsis progeny (P1), including enhanced germination, survival, and vegetative growth under high salinity. This adaptation requires recurrent stress exposure and is lost by the P2 generation after two stress-free generations.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C9 collectively describe a well-controlled multi-generational experiment with appropriate controls (C1-C3), clear phenotypic observations (C4-C5, C7), and consistent results showing that adaptation requires repeated stress (C6) and is transient (C7-C8). The experimental design minimizes confounding effects by timing stress application before flowering (C2) and uncoupling parent-progeny environments (C3). Statistical significance is reported in supplementary materials.

results.result: Transgenerational adaptation to hyperosmotic stress depends on DNA methylation machinery, as demonstrated by the lack of enhanced survival in progeny of stressed nrpd1a, cmt3, and rdd mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 present mutant analysis showing that disruption of DNA methylation pathways abolishes the adaptive response observed in wild-type. The use of multiple independent mutants affecting different components of the methylation machinery strengthens the conclusion. However, the claim acknowledges that phenotypic data alone do not reveal the extent of epigenetic changes (C11).

results.result: Whole-genome bisulfite sequencing reveals that hyperosmotic stress induces relatively few differentially methylated positions (DMPs) compared to previous reports, with stress-treated samples clustering separately from controls and showing predominantly methylation gains rather than losses.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C17 describe rigorous methylome analysis with appropriate replication (pooling 10 plants, duplicate samples) and statistical methods (C12-C14). The reanalysis of published data (C17) strengthens the finding that stress-induced methylation changes are more limited than previously reported. PCA and clustering analyses support the transient nature of methylation changes (C14-C15).

results.result: Hyperosmotic stress directs DNA methylation changes primarily to non-CG contexts (CHG and CHH) at differentially methylated regions (DMRs) located in transposable elements and intergenic regions near transcription start sites. These methylation patterns in P1 progeny correlate with adaptive phenotypes and revert to control levels in P2 progeny.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C25 present comprehensive DMR analysis with appropriate statistical testing (C21: P < 0.01, Student's t-test) and genomic annotation (C19). The correlation between methylation patterns and phenotypes across generations (C22-C24) is well-documented with clustering analysis. The focus on non-CG methylation contexts is consistent with known plant stress responses.

results.result: Approximately half of stress-induced DMRs (HS-DMRs) overlap with spontaneous epimutation-prone regions identified in mutation accumulation lines, indicating that hyperosmotic stress targets discrete, epigenetically labile genomic regions that are not randomly distributed.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C29 present comparative analysis with published MA line data showing substantial overlap (49%) despite methodological differences (pooled vs. individual plants). The enrichment of non-overlapping HS-DMRs near genes with stress-related functions (C28) supports the specificity of stress-induced changes. The inference that targeting is non-random (C27, C29) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Most HS-DMRs in G3 and G5 show hypermethylation in stressed plants, with enrichment near Helitrons (targeted by RdDM) for hypermethylated DMRs and near Copia, HAT, and Line L1 TEs (targeted by demethylases) for hypomethylated DMRs. These methylation changes gradually revert in P1 and P2 progeny, and drm1/drm2 mutants lack stress-induced hypermethylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C36 provide detailed characterization of DMR directionality and TE family associations with appropriate statistical testing (C32: p<0.01). The mutant analysis (C35) confirms RdDM involvement in hypermethylation. However, the lack of correlation with siRNA production (C36) suggests additional complexity in the mechanism that warrants further investigation.

results.result: HS-DMRs are enriched for stress-altered H3K27me3 histone modifications, with hypermethylated HS-DMRs showing an antagonistic relationship with H3K27me3 (decreased H3K27me3), indicating coordinated changes in DNA methylation and chromatin modifications at intergenic transposon-derived elements.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 integrate DNA methylation data with published histone modification data, showing substantial enrichment (63% vs. 13%) and an antagonistic relationship between repressive marks (C38). The authors appropriately note differences in experimental conditions between studies. The coordination of epigenetic marks supports a comprehensive model of stress-induced chromatin changes.

results.result: Enhanced tolerance to hyperosmotic stress is transmitted primarily through the female germline, and DME (DEMETER) DNA glycosylase activity in the male germline restricts paternal transmission by resetting stress-directed methylation marks, as demonstrated by enhanced stress tolerance in progeny of stressed dme-6 mutants and reciprocal crosses.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 present reciprocal cross experiments and mutant analysis showing parent-of-origin effects with appropriate statistical testing (C41: p<0.001). The use of reciprocal crosses with dme-6 mutants (C43) provides strong evidence for DME's role in restricting paternal transmission. The experimental design effectively tests the hypothesis about differential epigenetic resetting between gametes.

results.result: Methylome analysis of isolated sperm cells and vegetative nuclei reveals that hyperosmotic stress induces very few methylation changes in male gametes (only 3 DMRs), while 76% of HS-DMRs overlap with sperm-vegetative nucleus DMRs (SV-DMRs). In dme-6 mutants, HS-DMRs show altered methylation patterns, confirming DME's dual role in transposon silencing and resetting environmentally-induced epigenetic marks.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C50 present technically challenging gamete methylome analysis with appropriate cell sorting methodology (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The striking contrast between somatic and gametic methylation changes (C44-C45) and the substantial overlap with SV-DMRs (C46: 76%) support the conclusion about efficient resetting in male gametes. The dme-6 mutant analysis (C48) confirms DME's role, though the authors note that HS-DMRs are a subset of DME-regulated loci.

results.result: 123 genes flanked by HS-DMRs include 32% previously shown to be osmotic stress-responsive. The MYB20 gene, with an upstream HS-DMR that becomes hypermethylated in stressed P0 plants and maintained in P1, shows transgenerational downregulation in P1 and P2 progeny of stressed plants.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 link HS-DMRs to stress-responsive genes with appropriate comparative analysis using published expression data (C52). The detailed analysis of MYB20 methylation and expression across generations (C53-C54) with statistical significance (p=0.006) demonstrates a specific example of epigenetic regulation. The transgenerational expression changes correlate with methylation patterns.

results.result: The CNI1 gene has a downstream HS-DMR that becomes hypomethylated in P1 and P2 progeny of stressed plants, correlating with altered stress-responsive expression. Expression of CNI1 and other HS-DMR-associated genes is altered in rdd demethylation mutants and impaired in RdDM mutants, and methylation at HS-DMR regions is severely affected in met1 and rdd mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 present comprehensive analysis of CNI1 and additional genes with convergent evidence from methylation analysis, expression studies in wild-type and mutants, and analysis of published epigenomic data (C60: Fischer's Exact test p=0.005). The consistent findings across multiple genes and mutant backgrounds strengthen the conclusion about epigenetic regulation of stress-responsive genes.

results.result: T-DNA insertion alleles between CNI1 and its downstream HS-DMR show misregulated stress-responsive expression, and CRISPR/Cas9 deletion of the HS-DMR sequence reduces stress-induced downregulation of CNI1, demonstrating that the HS-DMR acts as a distant regulatory element.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 present strong functional evidence using independent insertion alleles and CRISPR/Cas9-generated deletions. The convergent results from multiple approaches (insertions disrupting communication and direct deletion) provide compelling evidence for the regulatory function of the HS-DMR. The experimental design appropriately tests the hypothesis about long-range regulation.

results.result: Inverted repeat (IR) hairpin transgenic lines that maintain methylation at the CNI1 HS-DMR even under hyperosmotic stress show loss of stress-induced CNI1 downregulation, demonstrating that the methylation status of the HS-DMR determines its regulatory activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 present gain-of-function experiments using IR hairpin constructs to force methylation, with confirmation by McrBC assays and bisulfite sequencing (C64). The loss of stress-responsive expression changes (C65) when methylation is maintained provides direct evidence that methylation status controls regulatory activity. This complements the loss-of-function experiments (C61-C63).

results.result: A long non-coding RNA (CNI1-AS1) transcribed antisense to CNI1 shows stress-dependent expression that differs between progeny of control and stressed plants. The stress responsiveness of CNI1-AS1 is impaired in rdd mutants and altered in insertion and deletion mutants, supporting a model where the HS-DMR acts as an epigenetic sensor controlling CNI1 expression through modulation of antisense lncRNA expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72 present a mechanistic model linking HS-DMR methylation to gene regulation via lncRNA with statistical support (C67: p=0.004; C68: p=0.015). The convergent evidence from wild-type, mutants, insertions, deletions, and IR hairpin lines (C69-C72) strongly supports the proposed mechanism. The model integrates multiple lines of evidence into a coherent regulatory framework.

results.result: Genome-wide analysis reveals that stress-responsive genes adjacent to HS-DMRs, but not MA-DMRs, are enriched for hyperosmotic-responsive antisense lncRNAs (Fisher's Exact test, p=0.008), indicating that HS-DMRs preferentially act as regulatory elements of stress-induced antisense lncRNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 extend the CNI1 findings to a broader genomic context with appropriate statistical testing. The specific enrichment for HS-DMRs versus MA-DMRs (C73) suggests that stress-induced methylation changes have distinct regulatory consequences compared to spontaneous epimutations. This supports the generalizability of the lncRNA regulatory mechanism.

results.result: The study concludes that intergenerational priming responses to hyperosmotic stress are triggered by recurrent exposure and rapidly lost without stress, involving targeted DNA methylation changes at discrete TE-rich genomic regions. These dynamic changes are functionally important (impaired in methylation mutants) and only a small fraction is transmitted to immediate offspring after recurrent stress, suggesting transient epigenetic stress memory in annual plants.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C79 synthesize the major findings into coherent conclusions supported by the experimental data. The characterization as 'transient' is well-supported by the P2 reversion data. The speculation about differences in perennial plants (C79) is appropriately qualified. The functional importance is demonstrated by mutant phenotypes (C77), though the authors acknowledge that mutants in different pathways show similar defects, suggesting complexity.

results.result: The study contextualizes findings by noting that half of stress-induced methylation changes overlap with epimutation-prone regions in MA lines, confirming epigenetically labile regions. Enhanced stress responses require two consecutive generations of exposure, explaining why previous single-episode studies failed to find inheritance. The limited number of epimutations suggests constrained epigenetic plasticity at key genomic regions potentially under purifying selection, with stress-specificity indicated by lack of overlap with other abiotic stress studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C87 place the findings in context of prior work with appropriate citations and comparative analysis. The explanation for discrepancies with previous studies (C82) is logical and supported by the data. The evolutionary interpretations (C86) and stress-specificity claims (C87) are appropriately qualified as suggestions. The overlap analysis with MA lines (C80, C84) provides quantitative support for the concept of labile regions.

results.result: The study discusses that hyperosmotic priming is transmitted primarily maternally because stress-associated methylation changes in leaves are largely absent in mature male gametes, indicating more efficient resetting in male versus female gametes. This involves DME-mediated active reprogramming at both transposon sequences and stress-dependent sites, with enhanced stress tolerance in dme-6 progeny implicating DME in dual roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C92 synthesize findings about parent-of-origin effects with mechanistic explanations based on gamete methylome data and mutant analysis. The inference about differential resetting efficiency (C90) is well-supported by the methylome data (C89). The dual role of DME (C92) is supported by both published literature (C91) and the current data (C41-C43, C48).

results.result: The authors propose an evolutionary explanation for maternal transmission based on plant reproductive biology: female gametes remain on the mother plant while pollen may travel long distances, and since seed dispersal is typically short-range, maternal transmission would efficiently retain relevant stress-associated adaptive responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 present evolutionary speculation based on general biological knowledge about plant reproduction (C93) and ecological reasoning (C94). While the logic is sound, this is a speculative explanation without direct experimental support. The manuscript appropriately presents this as 'one explanation' rather than a demonstrated mechanism. Additional experiments would be needed to test this hypothesis.

results.result: The discussion synthesizes that environmentally-induced priming involves DNA (de)methylation pathways controlling inheritance of epigenetic states, with stress specifically altering methylation at sequences adjacent to stress-response regulators. HS-DMRs are preferentially associated with antisense lncRNA transcription, and methylation changes could modulate transcription factor binding or chromatin loops, with TEs acting as epigenetic sensors.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C102 integrate the study's findings with published literature to propose mechanistic models. The core findings about DNA methylation pathways (C95-C96) and lncRNA associations (C99, C101) are well-supported by the experimental data. The mechanistic speculations about transcription factor binding and chromatin loops (C102) are appropriately qualified and cite relevant literature. Claims about TE regulatory roles (C97-C98) rely on cited literature.

results.result: The discussion considers evolutionary implications, noting that adaptive value of epigenetic inheritance depends on resetting costs and environmental predictability. In stochastic environments, bet-hedging via increased epigenetic variation could be advantageous, while the observed parental effects may be favored in relatively stable environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 present evolutionary theoretical considerations based on cited literature (Herman et al., 2014; Simons, 2011; Kuijper and Johnstone, 2016). While the discussion appropriately contextualizes the findings within evolutionary theory, these are speculative interpretations rather than experimentally tested hypotheses. The claims are appropriately qualified with conditional language ('could be', 'may be').
